body:
The Design page is where a human and a design agent work out how the software should look and be structured. Designs are reference material for the agents that build it.

**Goals:** ship something basic and working quickly while building toward a good long-term outcome, and make collaborative design between humans and agents possible.

## Reached when
- **Design has its own page**, not a tab in Strategy, with two tabs: **Architecture** and **UI/UX**.
- **A human designs with an agent**: they talk to a design agent in a panel like Strategy's planning panel, see its proposals drawn visually, and accept or reject them.
- **Designs can be cited**: each has a `design:<id>` that humans and agents can refer to, and any agent can read it while working.
- **Designs have history**: each accepted change saves a version, and a design can return to an earlier version without losing later ones.
- **Pointing is exact**: a human can point at an element or region, and an agent knows exactly what is meant by computation, without vision.
- **Designs can be built from**: a board task can name a design, and the agent turns it into working frontend code with few translation errors.
- **Direct editing works**: a human can drag a border, change a color, and eventually drag and drop components on both tabs.
- All linked features are complete.
- Every item under **To be determined** below is settled.

## To be determined before ending the milestone

### Questions
- What a tab's design list shows when it has no designs.
- What a row in a design's history shows, and how a restore is started.
- Whether a past version can be looked at before restoring it.
- How a design with several screens is arranged.
- Which components the default palette holds.
- Which tokens the default theme holds.
- Which variants each component has.
- How a click-through preview is started and left.
- How a proposal's highlights look, and how to see the current design while a proposal is open.
- Whether a design agent run belongs to one design or can move between several.

### Assumptions to confirm or overrule
- The agent panel sits opposite the left-hand list, as it does on Strategy.
- A removed element stays visible in a proposal, so the human can see what would go.
- An agent can't remove an Architecture node while edges still use it, unless it removes them too.

## Decided with the human
- **Design work is not task work.** Designing happens in conversation with the design agent, outside the board. Only building from a design is a task.
- **A design is reference material, not the source of truth for the code.** Agents base the frontend code on it. Solace does not regenerate code from it, because a design can go stale as soon as a feature adds a button or text, and regenerating could overwrite existing UI. Generating code directly stays an ideal for later, if it ever proves safe.
- **A design is data, not code.** It stays out of the symbol store and the Gleam and Rust type checks; Solace validates it with its own rules.
- **The element is the primitive.** An element is one component or container with a permanent ID, and it is to a design what a symbol is to code.
- **No text editor for humans.** The vision says humans work without reading code.
- **Designs belong to the workspace**, like Strategy, not to one project. A design may cover a small part of the workspace or use components shared across projects, and Solace itself is one app across 11 projects. A workspace holds many designs.
- **Agents change a design only through a proposal the human accepts.**
- **Notes only point.** A note is one or more element IDs plus text, sent with a chat message. A note that stays on a design is a narrative, which is not planned.

## Order
Features 1 to 4 (page and records, Architecture tab, UI/UX tab, design agent) are the first useful version. They depend on each other, because with no text editor the agent is the only way to create a design, so their order is settled when tasks are written. Then notes, building from a design, and direct editing. The process is expected to be iterative.

## Background
This came from goals and a four-stage plan the human brought from another agent, vetted against Solace in a Strategy conversation. That plan is direction, not gospel. Its four core requirements were: agents are fluent in the design's representation without relying on CSS; a user can point at a component or region and an agent can work out what is meant by computation; users can both drag and drop and edit what exists directly; and translating a design to Lustre is easy for agents and doesn't introduce errors.

## Left out
- **Not part of Design:** the plan's Strategy "Analysis" document, and deployment, which has its own milestone.
- **Dropped with code generation as the source of truth:** generated view modules that nobody edits, typed action parameters, a generated theme module, and checks that flag generated code drifting from the design.
- **Add when a real need appears:** grid and stack containers, sticky, scroll and overflow, screen states and mock data, attachments (raster images and SVG), an editable theme with "promote to token", a project's own component library as the palette, links from tasks to single elements, named versions, comparing versions, and branches.
- **Figma import** is a separate proposed feature outside this milestone, kept so the door stays open.
title: Design page rollout
